items.title: Sit Posture Classification using XGBoost Algorithm Based on Wearable Sensor Data
items.abstract: Prolonged non-ergonomic sitting posture during computer-based learning activities poses a risk of musculoskeletal disorders, yet current posture monitoring systems are largely static and neglect temporal aspects. This study develops a real-time posture classification system integrating accelerometer-based wearables with the XGBoost algorithm, specifically designed for university students. Data were collected from 21 subjects using two MPU6050 sensors placed on the thoracic and lumbar areas, yielding 28,054 data rows. Preprocessing involved mean imputation for missing values, removal of non-feature columns, and exclusion of gyroscope data due to extreme outliers. Feature extraction using 30-sample non-overlapping windows generated 24 statistical features (minimum, maximum, mean, standard deviation) from the accelerometer axes. As the primary benchmark for generalization, the XGBoost model was evaluated using Leave-One-Person-Out Cross-Validation (LOPOCV), achieving an average accuracy of 73.76% with balanced precision and recall scores (0.73–0.75), indicating consistent performance when encountering new subjects. Feature importance analysis identified az2_max (score: 0.1087) and az1_mean (score: 0.1053) as the most dominant features. Meanwhile, as an initial feasibility test under controlled conditions, real-time testing with five subjects (50 instances) reached 100% accuracy, with a web monitoring interface successfully displaying posture status, confidence values (53–81%), and posture-change logs, alongside a buzzer mechanism that activated appropriately upon detecting non-ergonomic postures. This system demonstrates the potential of low-cost accelerometer-based wearables for effective real-time posture monitoring; however, its performance is significantly influenced by individual physical characteristics such as height and weight. Consequently, future research is advised to diversify the dataset and implement personalization techniques to enhance generalization across broader populations.

items.title: Skin Cancer Detection and Classification: A Review of Recent Advances
items.abstract: Skin cancer is most common diseases find in humans worldwide and early detection can be assist to improve the doctors’ diagnosis. Traditional diagnosis depends on visual examination by dermatologists using dermoscopy also time consuming and depends heavily on the experience of the clinician or doctor. In recent years, deep learning has become the leading approach for automatic detection and classification skin lesions from dermoscopic and clinical images. In this paper we present a focused review of the most recent deep learning methods, published recently, for skin cancer detection and classification. The review covers benchmark datasets, image preprocessing and classification and segmentation methods, and major deep learning architectures, which include convolutional neural networks (CNNs), hybrid CNN-Transformer models, vision transformers, generative adversarial networks (GANs), and multimodal fusion approaches. It also summarizes the main challenges that still limit the real-world use of these systems, such as complex lesion features, image noise, intra-class variation, inter-class similarity, and class imbalance. In this paper we discuss future research directions, such as explainable artificial intelligence, fairness across different skin tones, and uncertainty-aware models. Keywords— Skin cancer; deep learning; dermoscopy; convolutional neural network; vision transformer; image classification; class imbalance

items.title: Smart Cities for Sustainable Urban Development Tejashri Prashant Jadhav
items.abstract: A smart city is defined as a city that employs communication and information technologies to enhance the entire process of governance, including making it more effective, public access to data, and enhancing the quality of government services alongside the well-being of citizens. Rapid population growth creates problems for cities associated with urban transport, air pollution, energy inefficiency, water scarcity, waste disposal issues, and burden on urban infrastructure. Smart city solutions include using new technologies, such as the Internet of Things (IoT), Artificial Intelligence (AI), Cloud Computing, Big Data Analytics, Geographic Information System (GIS), 5G, and intelligent sensors, for efficient resource management. Smart city technologies help monitor different aspects in real time and make intelligent decisions in the areas of transport, health, energy supply, waste management, and public safety. In India, the Smart Cities Mission has made cities implement several technology-based initiatives for sustainable development and citizen engagement. In this research paper, the concept, design, technologies, applications, advantages, problems and perspectives of smart cities are examined, taking into account their applications in India.

items.title: Smart cities require smarter crime prevention methodologies: Integrating AI within urban safety frameworks
items.abstract: ABSTRACT. As urban areas transform into intelligent ecosystems, artificial intelligence technologies are assuming an increasingly vital role in the prevention of urban crime. This research amalgamates artificial intelligence with conventional criminological theories, specifically Routine Activity Theory (RAT) and Crime Pattern Theory (CPT) to theorize framework and practical approaches to urban crime prevention. To methodically evaluate the convergence of artificial intelligence implementation in urban crime deterrence. AI implements predictive policing and real-time monitoring, establishing a novel kind of oversight that perpetually observes metropolitan environments, hence diminishing prospects for criminal activity. This study contends that multidisciplinary methodologies for urban crime prevention, integrating technology with social and spatial theories, yield more successful and nuanced solutions. The findings convey a definitive message: although technology and urban design are significant, the primary emphasis for effective crime prevention is in education, preventive measures, and the strategic integration of digital tools.

items.title: Smart Farming in Arid Lands: AI and Digital Innovation in Sangola's Pomegranate Economy
items.abstract: Abstract The global community stands at a critical crossroads where technological advancement and environmental preservation must converge to ensure human well-being. This paper explores the multidisciplinary approach required to navigate global futures, focusing on the harmonization of economic science, Artificial Intelligence (AI), and digital innovation with sustainability metrics. Focusing specifically on the drought-prone Sangola Taluka of Solapur District, Maharashtra, this study examines how traditional agrarian economies can transition into sustainable models using precision farming. With over 73.96% of the workforce in Solapur engaged in agriculture, yet suffering from an average rainfall of less than 545-750 mm, integrating AI-driven resource frameworks is crucial. The paper provides factual insights into the pomegranate economy of Sangola and highlights how digital interventions can optimize water use, mitigate economic risks, and align local systems with Environmental Sustainability. Critical interventions such as IoT sensors, Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) for pathological tracking, and decentralized drone application systems are detailed to model an optimal input-to-output agricultural grid.

items.title: Smart Farming Using Applications of Artificial Intelligence
items.abstract: Abstract Agriculture is one of the key sectors in the global economy and is a key component of food security, rural employment and sustainable development. But, there are certain serious problems in the modern agriculture like climate change, scarcity of water, degradation of soil, rise in production cost, labour scarcity, crop diseases, attack by pests, and food demands. The collection of periodic observations and experience of traditional farming methods may not always be sufficient and reliable information for making complex decision making in agriculture. Smart farming, with the assistance of Artificial Intelligence (AI), can be a data-driven solution to solve these challenges. With AI, one can gather and process vast amounts of data from sensors, satellites, drones, weather stations, farming equipment, and mobile devices, and then take action on that information. The use of machine learning, deep learning, computer vision, robotics, Internet of Things (IoT), predictive analytics and decision-support systems is gaining traction in agriculture. These technologies can help farmers in the selection of crops, soil testing, precision irrigation, fertilizer management, pest/disease detection, yield prediction, weed management, harvesting, livestock monitoring, and supply-chain management. This research paper reviews the significant applications of Artificial Intelligence in smart farming, its benefits, technical architecture, challenges and future prospects. The study was conducted based on the analysis of recent studies published in the literature on 6R (AI, Precision Agriculture, AIoT, Smart Irrigation, Remote Sensing, and Machine Learning). Recent systematic reviews suggest crop monitoring, irrigation, pest and disease management, yield prediction, nutrient management, robotics, and protected cultivation are key areas where AI is applicable. The paper concludes that with the proper infrastructure, farmer training, reliable data, and affordable technologies, AI can play a significant role in productive, efficient, climate-resilient, and sustainable agriculture.

items.title: SmartLab: AI-Based College Laboratory Equipment Tracking and Predictive Maintenance System
items.abstract: College laboratories contain equipment that must be identified, tracked, and maintained to support practical learning. Manual registers and periodic inspections can make it difficult to know the current status of each item, find maintenance history quickly, and identify equipment that may need servicing. SmartLab proposes a software-based system for registering laboratory equipment, tracking its status, maintaining service records, and using equipment usage and maintenance history to estimate maintenance needs. The application provides a staff dashboard for equipment registration, tracking, maintenance updates, and reports. Equipment can be assigned a unique ID and a status such as Available, In Use, Faulty, or Under Maintenance. A predictive-maintenance module can analyse recorded usage and service history to flag equipment for inspection. The system is intended to improve record accessibility, support timely maintenance, and reduce avoidable disruption in college laboratories. Predictions are decision-support suggestions and should be verified by laboratory staff. Keywords: SmartLab, laboratory equipment tracking, predictive maintenance, artificial intelligence, equipment management, maintenance history.

items.title: Social and Pedagogical Drivers of ChatGPT Acceptance: An Extended TAM Model in Teacher Education
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence tools, particularly applications such as ChatGPT, hold significant potential to reshape the landscape of teacher education by offering opportunities for personalized feedback and adaptive learning. These tools also play important roles in teachers’ pedagogical decisions while designing their teachings in present learning environments. However, the underlying mechanisms driving pre-service teachers’ adoption of such particular tools remain under-explored. This study addresses this gap by validating an extended technology acceptance model incorporating constructivist teaching beliefs, subjective norms, facilitating conditions, ChatGPT self-efficacy, and perceived enjoyment. Data collected from 488 senior pre-service teachers in Türkiye were analyzed using structural equation modeling. Results show that ChatGPT self-efficacy and perceived enjoyment significantly predict perceived ease of use, whereas facilitating conditions do not exert a significant influence. Perceived usefulness is significantly associated with perceived ease of use, subjective norms, and pedagogical beliefs. Behavioral intention is significantly associated with perceived usefulness, subjective norms, and ChatGPT self-efficacy, with the framework explaining 54% of the variance. Given the cross-sectional nature of the data, these results offer tentative implications for teacher education. Practically, the findings highlight the potential value of scaffolded micro-teaching and institutional verification procedures for supporting responsible and equitable generative AI use in teacher education. Further recommendations are discussed in the light of teacher education procedures and policies.

items.title: Social Media and Motivation Influencing Thai Tourists' Revisit Intention to Bangkok's Nostalgic Cultural Destinations
items.abstract: This study investigates the influence of Social Media Influence, Push Motivation, and PullMotivation on Thai tourists’ intention to revisit nostalgic cultural destinations in Bangkok, Thailand.Using a quantitative research approach, data were collected from 440 Thai tourists visiting Wat Arun,Wat Pho, and the Grand Palace. The conceptual framework was analyzed using Partial Least SquaresStructural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM) with SmartPLS. The results indicate that Social MediaInfluence had the strongest influence on revisit intention (β = 0.462, p < 0.001), followed by PushMotivation (β = 0.296, p < 0.001). In contrast, Pull Motivation did not significantly influence revisitintention (β = 0.056, p = 0.475). The model explained 40.0% of the variance in revisit intention (R² =0.400). These findings indicate that social media influence and intrinsic motivational factors areassociated with tourists’ intention to revisit, while destination-related pull motivation was notsignificant in this study. The study contributes to research on nostalgic cultural tourism and providespractical implications for destination managers and tourism marketers seeking to strengthen revisitintention through social media communication and culturally engaging experiences.

items.title: Standard and decoupled knowledge distillation for lightweight radiographic knee osteoarthritis grading and triage
items.abstract: Abstract This retrospective study compares standard knowledge distillation (KD) and decoupled knowledge distillation (DKD) fo​r lightweight artificial intelligence-based​ radiographic knee osteoarthritis grading. GhostNetV2 students learned five Kellgren–Lawrence grades from a Swin-Tiny teacher and were evaluated against a cross-entropy baseline using an Osteoarthritis Initiative-derived dataset of 8260 images from 4130 patients with patient-disjoint partitions. Across three​ runs, mean binary triage accuracy was 84.04%, 84.82%, and 84.82% for baseline, standard KD, and DKD. Thresholds targeting at least 90% validation specificity yielded test sensitivities of 72.77%, 76.56%, and 75.50%, with specificities of 92.09%, 90.94%, and 91.12%; these operating points are not specificity-matched. Mean five-class accuracy was 64.63%, 67.63%, and 67.71%. Separate illustrative checkpoints showed reduced KL-1-to-KL-2 overcalls with DKD (28.0 to 18.9%) but lower KL-0 recall (90.6 to 78.7%). Calibration, exploratory decision curves, and patient-cluster uncertainty intervals were evaluated. Each student contains 4.88 million parameters. Distillation improved mean performance internally, but decoupling did not demonstrate an additional sensitivity benefit over standard KD. No external cohort or clinician-supported decision policy was evaluated; clinical utility and population-level stability remain unestablished.

items.title: Starting Again from Human Needs: The Organismic Foundation of Jean-Pol Martin's New Human Rights
items.abstract: What changes when our conception of the human being becomes the starting point for rethinking society? This conceptual paper explains in what sense Jean-Pol Martin’s New Human Rights (NHR; German: Neue Menschenrechte, NMR) propose such a new beginning. The framework takes the living, thinking, social and meaning-oriented human organism as its reference point. Six interdependent and equally ranked basic needs guide the assessment of social arrangements: thinking, health, security, social inclusion, self-realization and participation, and meaning. Thinking also performs a central regulatory function through information processing, conceptualization and anticipation. The paper’s specific contribution is to make this organismic foundation explicit and clarify its consequences for the justification of institutions. Schools, public administrations and workplaces are examined in relation to the conditions they provide for maintaining and developing human life. Learning by Teaching (LdL) illustrates how this conception of the human being can inform educational practice. Within Martin’s publication series, the article connects the anthropological foundation of NHR with institutional evaluation and participatory social design. It also outlines an open programme of collective inquiry for the emerging school of thought. The article reconstructs and clarifies an existing theoretical framework; it does not report a new empirical study or claim historical priority. Conceptual basis: Jean-Pol Martin. items.title: StyloBuddy: A Hybrid Deep Learning and LLM Framework for Trend-Aware Outfit Recommendation
items.abstract: StyloBuddy is an outfit recommendation system that pairs deep visual compatibility scoring with large language model (LLM) reasoning and trend-aware catalogue enrichment. It has four components: (1) a GPT-4o Vision Pipeline for zero-shot clothing attribute extraction; (2) a Type-Aware Compatibility Network (TACN) trained on 15,000 synthetic outfit pairs from the Fashion Product Images dataset, which scores outfit compatibility through category-specific subspaces; (3) a Three-Mode Recommendation Engine that routes requests through three paths (online, auto-suggest, and offline fallback), with 97.3% prompt compliance; and (4) a prototyped Apify-based Trend Scraping Pipeline for periodic catalogue enrichment. The hybrid pipeline is deployed in production: for large item selections (6 or more items), TACN scores all upper-lower pairs and passes only the top-ranked combinations to GPT-4o, cutting LLM input by up to 75% while preserving recommendation quality. We report a comparative analysis (p < 0.01, Fleiss' kappa = 0.73), an ablation study, and a user study (N=45, mean satisfaction 4.12/5.0). This is a technical report and has not been peer reviewed.

items.title: SUPPORTING CASE ANALYSIS THROUGH GUIDED LLM PROMPTING IN Online CASE-BASED MARKETING COURSES: AN EXPLORATOYR CLASSROOM-BASED COMPARISON
items.abstract: The Case Method trains students to define managerial problems, compare alternatives, and defend recommendations under uncertainty. Preserving these processes online can be difficult, and large language models (LLMs) further complicate this challenge by enabling students to generate “polished” recommendations without constructively engaging in the Case Method. Using the ICAP framework as a design lens, we developed a guided LLM prompting marketing case assignment requiring students to evaluate multiple LLM-generated alternatives before synthesizing their own recommendation. We then conducted a classroom-based comparison across three online sections: asynchronous with guided LLM intervention, asynchronous without guided LLM intervention, and hybrid without guided LLM intervention but with synchronous discussion and debrief. Students in the guided LLM prompting format self-reported higher perceived self-directed learning than students in the two comparison formats, although uncertainty around the effect-size estimate warrants cautious interpretation. No significant omnibus differences emerged for perceived collaborative learning, problem solving, or critical thinking, indicating that guided LLM prompting should not be assumed to improve all dimensions of case-based learning. Findings suggest that this assignment may be most useful as a targeted pedagogical structure for supporting independent case analysis and offer educators a practical framework for aligning LLM use with specific Case Method learning processes.

items.title: Sustained use of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) in programming education: a systematic review of empirical evidence on adoption, learning outcomes, and continuance intention
items.abstract: This systematic review explores how Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) technologies have been adopted and sustained within programming education from 2023 to 2025, uncovering their applications, educational benefits, and challenges. This review draws on 45 empirical studies identified through five major academic databases, including Scopus, Web of Science, IEEE Xplore, SpringerLink, and Google Scholar. The analysis reveals that GenAI could enhance programming education by supporting code generation, debugging assistance, personalised explanations, feedback provision, and learner engagement. However, key challenges remain concerning inaccurate outputs, academic integrity, learner dependency, trust, and unequal access to AI-supported learning resources. This study suggests that educators should strategically employ GenAI as a complementary learning resource, maximising its educational benefits while addressing potential limitations. The findings highlight the importance of educator preparation, institutional guidance, and responsible AI integration, while future research should further investigate long-term continuance intention behaviour, comparative effectiveness of emerging GenAI programming tools, and sustainable implementation strategies across diverse educational contexts.

items.title: Task Context Shapes Ocular Associations with Stress, Cognitive Workload, and Fatigue: A Wearable Eye-Tracking Study
items.abstract: Background: Eye-tracking correlations with cognitive and emotional states vary across studies, likely because they depend on specific task demands. We investigated the consistency and specificity of such associations between wearable eye-tracking data and self-reported measures of stress, cognitive workload, and fatigue within assessment-centre-style tasks.Methods: Participants performed tasks involving social evaluation, reasoning, planning, comprehension, and presentation while wearing Meta Aria Gen 1 glasses. Data from 97 participants were analysed using linear mixed-effects models to examine associations between 104 wearable eye-tracking and head-movement metrics and each self-reported state, while accounting for task effects. Metric-by-task interactions assessed task dependence, and sensitivity analyses examined the effects of elapsed session time and shared variance among states.Results: After false-discovery-rate correction, significant metric-by-task interactions were observed in 53 stress, 61 workload, and 12 fatigue models, especially for saccade amplitude, speed, and duration. Across tasks, stress was linked to increased gaze variability, while workload and fatigue were linked to greater fixation angular distance. Fatigue associations weakened after adjusting for session time, and no fatigue metric-by-task interactions remained significant after adjustment for elapsed session time. After controlling for overlap among self-reported states, associations remained significant for stress, but not workload or fatigue.Conclusion: Ocular associations varied by task and by the shared variance across subjective states. Measures of fixation distribution appeared to capture a more general subjective-state component rather than exclusively distinguishing workload or fatigue. Several gaze and saccade associations with stress remained significant after adjustment for workload and fatigue. Predictive modelling should distinguish shared from state-specific information and be validated across diverse activities.

items.title: Teachers’ Classroom and Instructional Management, and Students’ Learning Engagement
items.abstract: This study examined the classroom and instructional management practices of new and experienced teachers and their relationship with students’ learning engagement in selected public secondary schools in Cortes District, Division of Bohol, during School Year 2026–2027. Anchored in the Classroom Management Scripts Model, Instructional Clarity Framework, Multidimensional Student Engagement Framework, and Huberman’s Teacher Career Cycle, the study employed a quantitative comparative-correlational research design. Respondents comprised 15 new teachers, 46 experienced teachers, and 278 students, totaling 339 participants. Data were gathered using a researcher-modified, validated, and pilot-tested questionnaire and analyzed through descriptive statistics, Pearson product–moment correlation, and independent-samples t-tests. Results revealed consistently high classroom and instructional management practices among both teacher groups, with no statistically significant differences. Classroom management and instructional management exhibited a strong positive relationship (r = 0.724, p < 0.001), whereas neither classroom management (r = 0.040, p = 0.760) nor instructional management (r = −0.062, p = 0.635) was significantly associated with students’ overall learning engagement. Students taught by new teachers demonstrated significantly higher overall and emotional engagement (p = 0.017), while behavioral and cognitive engagement showed no significant differences. The study concluded that teaching experience alone does not determine management effectiveness and that favorable management practices do not necessarily correspond to higher student engagement. A school-based professional development program emphasizing mentoring, collaborative lesson planning, peer observation, and instructional improvement was proposed. The study supports Sustainable Development Goal 4 (Quality Education) by promoting effective teaching, inclusive learning environments, and continuous professional growth. Its educational and institutional sustainability contribution lies in providing localized evidence to guide sustained professional development and improvements in students’ learning experiences.

items.title: Technology acceptance mediates associations between pre-service physical education teachers’ AI-TPACK and study engagement and behavioral intentions in digital teaching
items.abstract: Abstract Against the backdrop of artificial intelligence (AI) reshaping the educational landscape, the digital transformation of physical education has placed greater demands on preservice physical education teachers’ (PSPETs’) capacity to integrate technology. However, research remains limited on the effects of pres-ervice physical education teachers’ artificial intelligence technological pedagogical content knowledge (PSPETs AI-TPACK) on their study engagement (SE) and behavioral intentions (BI) in digital teaching, as well as on the role played by technology acceptance (TA) in these relationships.This study involved 1,144 undergraduate and postgraduate students enrolled in physical education, physical education teaching, or physical education and training programmes at five higher education institutions in Guangzhou, Guangdong Province. Using adapted scales, data were collected on PSPETs AI-TPACK, TA, SE, and BI. Structural equation modelling (SEM) was then employed to examine the relationships among these variables and the mediating effects. The findings showed that PSPETs AI-TPACK significantly and positively predicted both SE and BI in digital teaching. TA played a significant partial mediating role in the relationships between PSPETs AI-TPACK and SE, and between PSPETs AI-TPACK and BI. These results indicate that PSPETs AI-TPACK can promote PSPETs’ SE and BI both directly and indirectly by enhancing their TA. This study extends the theoretical understanding of the relationships between PSPETs AI-TPACK and SE and BI in digital physical education teaching, while also providing empirical evidence for improving preservice physical education teacher education in higher education institutions. Higher education institutions should incorporate AI-based instructional design and practice into physical education teacher education curricula, implement tiered and progressive technology training, create authentic digital teaching contexts, and enhance PSPETs’ TA through resource provision and exemplary applications. These measures can, in turn, strengthen PSPETs’ SE and BI in using AI technologies to support physical education teaching.

items.title: Technology and Communication in the Age of Artificial Intelligence: Reimagining English for Global Futures
items.abstract: Abstract Technology has changed the way people use language and communicate with one another. The growth of the internet, smartphones, social media and artificial intelligence has brought major changes in the way we read, write, speak and share information. English, being widely used in education, business, science and international communication, has been greatly influenced by these changes. Today, communication is not limited to books, classrooms or face-to-face conversations. People communicate through emails, social media, video calls, online classes, digital presentations and AI-based tools. This paper examines the changing relationship between language, technology and communication, with special focus on English. It discusses how digital technology has influenced English language use and how artificial intelligence is becoming part of language learning and communication. The paper also looks at the advantages and problems of using AI in English education. AI tools can help learners improve their vocabulary, grammar, writing and communication skills. At the same time, too much dependence on such tools may affect independent thinking, creativity and originality. The paper argues that technology should support human communication rather than replace it. English education should therefore help learners develop language skills along with digital literacy, critical thinking, creativity and responsible use of technology. The paper concludes that preparing students for the future requires a balanced approach in which technology and human abilities work together.

items.title: Testing for Deriving Observable State of Software Systems
items.abstract: Software tests commonly verify selected behavior under controlled conditions. Production operation poses another question: can responsible observers determine what happened, when, under which authority, with which effects, and within what uncertainty? A system can pass behavioral tests while its receipts, event transport, storage, derivations, health indicators, or observation surfaces are missing, stale, corrupted, misleading, or inaccessible. This paper develops Testing as Observability Expansion within the proposed DSS:OS:TEST domain. It treats a test as a bounded evidence artifact supporting a declared claim under a scenario, environment, oracle, observation regime, and inference range. Tests do not generally prove that software "can be known"; they can test specified links in an evidence path and reveal untested or failed regions. The revised architecture replaces an absolute evidence hierarchy with a dependency graph, treats seven evidence classes as overlapping facets, defines an evidence-path contract and a Constitutional Test Runner report, and makes observability closure relative to a declared claim inventory and profile. It integrates witness semantics, receipt-based reasoning, epistemic situational awareness, and meta-binding tests while preserving their distinct roles.

items.title: THE ALGORITHMIC SKINNER BOX: A PHCA SYSTEMS AUDIT OF REINFORCEMENT SCHEDULES, COMPUTATIONAL ARCHITECTURE, AND COGNITIVE AUTONOMY
items.abstract: THE ALGORITHMIC SKINNER BOX: A PHCA SYSTEMS AUDIT OF REINFORCEMENT SCHEDULES, COMPUTATIONAL ARCHITECTURE, AND COGNITIVE AUTONOMY Executive Summary & Abstract For nearly a century, B.F. Skinner’s theory of operant conditioning has shaped our understanding of human behavior. The core premise is simple: behavior is shaped by consequences—rewards and punishments. But in the modern era, the environment shaping human behavior is no longer a physical laboratory. It is an adaptive, algorithmic architecture. This paper proposes the Algorithmic Skinner Box as a systems-level model to examine the precise interaction between digital reinforcement schedules, algorithmic personalization, and the measurable degradation of human autonomy. We do not assume that all digital platforms universally produce neurochemical addiction. Instead, we distinguish between specific mechanisms of behavioral conditioning. We analyze the difference between Variable-Ratio (VR) schedules (reinforcement after an unpredictable number of actions), Variable-Interval (VI) schedules (reinforcement after unpredictable time intervals), and the complex Mixed Schedules utilized by modern social media and digital feeds. By applying the Proclean Hierarchical Constraint Architecture (PHCA), we map how adaptive computational systems observe user behavior, modify subsequent stimuli, and optimize engagement through continuous feedback loops. This is the Dioptopticon—an architecture of attention capture that operates without the need for physical coercion. However, this paper explicitly separates observable behavioral conditioning from unverified neurobiological claims. We do not assert that dopamine is a simple "pleasure chemical" being hijacked. Instead, we map dopaminergic reward prediction errors and motivational salience, proposing a rigorous research program to determine exactly how externally controlled reinforcement contingencies alter behavioral response frequency and attentional allocation. The Dynamic System Model To formalize this, we abandon the static metaphors of the past and model the human-algorithm interaction as a dynamic state-space system. We identify four measurable variables: · Attentional Allocation · Compulsive Engagement Frequency · Intrinsic Motivational Orientation · Behavioral Response Sensitivity to External Reinforcement This model defines the platform not as a passive tool, but as a coupled computational system that interacts with the human nervous system in real-time. The Falsification Protocol This is a scientific audit, not a conspiracy theory. The paper proposes five falsifiable hypotheses (H1–H5) to empirically test the effects of these reinforcement schedules. We demand longitudinal testing of executive function, rigorous measurement of withdrawal-related distress, and controlled experiments comparing voluntary engagement against algorithmic compulsion. If traditional behavioral economics explains these phenomena better than the PHCA model, the math must yield to the evidence. Sovereign Cognition: The Architectural Reform We cannot solve algorithmic capture with simple "dopamine detoxes." We must fundamentally redefine psychological autonomy. This paper introduces Sovereign Cognition as an operational construct: Sovereign Cognition is the measurable capacity of an individual to initiate, sustain, interrupt, and redirect goal-directed behavior independently of externally imposed reinforcement contingencies. To restore cognitive sovereignty, we must measure and architect for four dimensions: the ability to Initiate a self-selected task, the ability to Persist in the face of distraction, the ability to Interrupt external stimuli, and the ability to Redirect attention based on internal goals. The Bottom Line A digital system should not be evaluated solely by how effectively it captures attention, but by whether its users retain the ability to withdraw that attention voluntarily. The legacy system engineered a Skinner Box in your pocket. The PHCA framework provides the tools to measure the constraints, expose the feedback loops, and engineer a sovereign way out. The signal is not absolute. The evidence determines its strength. Solve et coagula. — Anthony J. Blair Founder, Proclus Dynamics Consortium

items.title: THE ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE REVOLUTION IN FINANCE: FROM ALGORITHMS TO STRATEGIC SOLUTIONS
items.abstract: A rapid development of artificial intelligence (AI) technologies is transforming the financial sector, changing approaches to automating operations, analyzing data bulk, forecasting, risk management, customer service, and making management decisions. The relevance of the study is due to the need to transition from the fragmented and predominantly operational use of algorithmic tools to their systemic integration into strategic management in finance. The purpose of the study is to systematize the areas of application of AI in the financial sector and substantiate the conceptual model of the transition from the operational use of algorithmic tools to the strategic level of management. To achieve the set goal, systemic, historical-logical, comparative, and classification methods were used. The main results of the study are the identification of four stages of the evolution of AI applications in finance: algorithmic-rule, machine learning, deep learning, and generative-strategic. The key areas of AI use are systematized by the level of managerial influence - from the automation of routine operations and support of individual business processes to forecasting, risk management, personalization of financial services, and the formation of strategic management decisions. The technological, regulatory, reputational, ethical, and systemic risks associated with scaling AI in the financial sector are summarized. A five-level maturity model of AI application is proposed, which involves a sequential transition from experimental, operational, and integrated levels to the level of managerial transformation and strategic use of technologies.It is concluded that the strategic value of AI is determined not by the number of implemented technological solutions, but by the degree of their integration into the corporate governance system, the quality and availability of data, the effectiveness of model management, personnel competencies, the explainability of algorithmic solutions, compliance with regulatory requirements, and the effectiveness of risk control. The strategic integration of AI creates the prerequisites for increasing the adaptability, competitiveness, and sustainability of the financial sector.

This study examines changes in higher education leadership responses to AI through publicly available institutional policies, guidelines, governance reports, and strategic communications from 11 universities. It considers institutional responses across four analytical periods: emergence, adaptation, integration, and institutionalization. The study contributes to higher education leadership research by examining how institutional AI guidance has developed and how universities have addressed academic integrity, ethical use, AI literacy, teaching and learning, and institutional governance. I welcome researchers, educators, and higher education professionals to read, share, and engage with this study.

items.title: The Coordinates of Thought: A Question-Centered Architecture for Comparative Philosophy
items.abstract: The Coordinates of Thought: A Question-Centered Architecture for Comparative Philosophy presents the intellectual framework, classification methodology, and digital continuation of The Coordinates of Thought — Philosophy: Every Question, Answer, Thinker and Tradition, an unpublished philosophical reference book by Syed Raheel Shahzad, prepared under the publishing imprint of The Syed Group. Syed Raheel Shahzad is an author, business strategist, and systems thinker whose writing examines philosophy, knowledge, reasoning, human understanding, civilization, and the architecture of complex systems. His approach emphasizes the relationships between questions, assumptions, arguments, competing explanations, and the intellectual structures through which human understanding develops. The Coordinates of Thought applies this systems-oriented approach to the organization, study, comparison, and navigation of world philosophy. The central problem addressed by the work is the fragmentation of philosophical knowledge. Traditional histories commonly organize philosophy chronologically, encyclopedias organize it alphabetically, and specialized disciplines frequently examine ideas within separate conceptual boundaries. Although each method serves an important purpose, readers may struggle to identify how philosophical questions connect to competing answers, which thinkers advanced particular positions, where disagreements arise, and how different intellectual traditions approached comparable problems. The book proposes a question-centered architecture of philosophical inquiry organized through four interconnected coordinates: Question, Answer, Thinker, and Tradition. This framework seeks to transform philosophical knowledge from a collection of disconnected subjects, historical names, and schools into a navigable intellectual reference system. At its foundation is an original taxonomy of 131 philosophical questions organized under six principal roots: Metaphysics, Epistemology, Ethics and Axiology, Logic, Aesthetics, and the Philosophy of Specialized Fields. Its decimal addressing system establishes relationships between foundational questions, subordinate problems, and neighboring domains of inquiry. Questions concerning existence, causation, consciousness, personal identity, free will, knowledge, justification, truth, moral responsibility, justice, reasoning, beauty, political authority, artificial intelligence, death, and meaning are located within this connected structure. A second dimension maps philosophical positions and their alternatives. Rather than presenting individual doctrines in isolation, the framework compares competing answers through their underlying assumptions, points of disagreement, conceptual consequences, objections, and explanatory limitations. Distinctions between realism and anti-realism, determinism and free will, foundationalism and coherentism, and other major philosophical positions become part of a broader architecture of disagreement. The book's comparative-historical component places seven philosophical traditions on a parallel timeline, examining intellectual developments, philosophical exchanges, historical contexts, and the transmission of ideas. It challenges the assumption that world philosophy can be adequately understood through a single European historical sequence. Indian, Chinese, Greek, Islamic, Jewish, European, and other intellectual developments are examined through attention to historical evidence, translation, conceptual differences, and the limitations of cross-cultural comparison. Its principal structure includes a guide to philosophical navigation, the branch taxonomy, comparative position maps, a parallel historical timeline, and cross-tradition examinations of ten fundamental philosophical questions. Supporting materials include conceptual indexes, thinker pathways, comparative reference tools, bibliographic resources, and methodological explanations. The framework distinguishes between representing a philosophical position and endorsing it, preserving disagreement where philosophical questions remain unresolved. The research continues beyond the book through Coordinates of Thought, a connected digital philosophy, education, and reference platform founded by Syed Raheel Shahzad. The website extends the book-derived question system into a growing knowledge environment linking philosophical questions, thinkers, traditions, schools, concepts, books, arguments, and historical contexts. The digital platform includes the 131 interconnected question cards, more than 700 thinker entries, philosophical subject guides, a philosophy glossary, a growing book and bibliography collection, structured reading pathways, and the World Philosophy Atlas, which connects thinkers and philosophical developments to geographical locations, timelines, intellectual journeys, and the historical transmission of ideas. For learning and participation, the platform organizes discussion across nine philosophical subjects and 67 thematic parts. Its educational and community components include introductory learning resources, a philosophy journal, reader discussions, philosophical debates, open questions, and reading groups. These functions are intended to support multiple approaches to inquiry, from introductory exploration to more advanced comparative study. The digital continuation also develops a source-aware reference framework through bibliographic attribution, links to primary and secondary scholarship, citation guidance, editorial standards, and documented corrections. The original book-derived taxonomy remains distinguishable from independently developed editorial material and community contributions. This distinction is essential to preserving authorship, historical accountability, and the integrity of the expanding knowledge system. The relationship between the book and the website is therefore complementary rather than duplicative. The book supplies the proposed intellectual architecture; the digital platform provides an evolving environment for navigating, connecting, studying, questioning, and extending that architecture. Readers may begin with a philosophical question, examine rival positions, identify relevant thinkers, consult historical and bibliographic sources, explore cross-tradition relationships, and continue inquiry through learning and discussion. The contribution described in this research overview is an author-proposed framework for philosophical classification, comparative inquiry, and digital knowledge organization. It does not claim to establish a universally accepted taxonomy, replace original philosophical texts, or resolve the disagreements that constitute philosophical inquiry. The broader objective is to develop Coordinates of Thought as an enduring, internationally accessible home for philosophy, supporting readers, students, educators, researchers, and institutions through connected philosophical knowledge, responsible citation, intellectual accessibility, and continuing critical inquiry. This document is a publicly available research overview of the framework and its digital continuation. It is not the complete unpublished book or a reproduction of its manuscript.

items.title: The Dual-Edged Sword of Automation: Assessing the Role of Artificial Intelligence in Accelerating and Inhibiting Sustainable Development
items.abstract: Abstract Artificial Intelligence (AI) has emerged as a fundamental catalyst for transformation across global societies, fundamentally altering the pathways available to achieve the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). This paper presents a critical, socio-technical review of AI's dual role as both an enabler and an inhibitor of sustainability. Synthesizing recent macro-level consensus frameworks and empirical case studies, we demonstrate that while machine learning architectures optimize resource efficiency, power smart grids, and augment climate tracking, they simultaneously expose systemic vulnerabilities. These include severe ecological footprints driven by the energy-water nexus of hyperscale data centers, algorithmic bias that exacerbates socio-economic inequality, and a compounding interdisciplinary 'expertise gap.' This paper maps these dual-impact nodes across environmental, social, and economic dimensions, concluding with actionable governance strategies designed to guide policy toward a balanced digital-green transition.

items.title: The Economics and Operations of Lights-Out Manufacturing: A Comprehensive Analysis of Dark Factories in the Industry 4.0 Era
items.abstract: Abstract Industry 4.0 has brought about a paradigm shift of global production systems from traditional manufacturing to highly automated ecosystems. The pièce de résistance of this evolution is the "Dark Factory" or "Lights-Out Manufacturing", which refers to a production facility that is designed to run unattended with little to no human intervention throughout the entire process. This study investigates in the secondary data collected from industry reports, academic literature and corporate case studies contexts of dark factories technological framework, their economic potential and scalable operating aspects. Analysis uses data from 2013 to October 2025. Results indicate that fully dark factories remain a niche implementation limited mostly to high volume, high precision industries; however, "semi-dark" environments are being established based on the advances of Artificial intelligence (AI), Industrial Internet of Things (IIoT), and advanced robotics. The study comes to the conclusion that, continuous uninterrupted production and low variable overheads cost providing the massive economic benefits to the manufacturing industries. But at the same time the management must overcome the major challenges related to the cyber vulnerabilities, large initial investments and the socioeconomic effects of workforce relocation.

items.title: THE EVOLUTION OF THE ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE CHARACTER IN TWENTIETH- AND TWENTY-FIRST-CENTURY AMERICAN LITERATURE
items.abstract: This article traces the evolution of the artificial intelligence character in American prose fiction from the beginning of the twentieth century to the 2020s by examining four classical instruments of literary characterization: portrait, dialogue, landscape, and monologue. Drawing on Mikhail Bakhtin’s theories of dialogism and of the author’s “excess of seeing,” Jurij Lotman’s semiotics of artistic space, the Russian Formalist concepts of the dominant and of literary evolution, Dorrit Cohn’s narratology of consciousness, and posthumanist criticism, the study argues that the history of the artificial character in American literature can be read as a gradual migration of narrative authority from human to machine. In the first half of the century, in the works of Baum, del Rey, Asimov, and Williamson, the machine is chiefly an object of portraiture, measured by the human gaze against the human body. After the “imitation game” proposed by Alan Turing in 1950, dialogue becomes dominant, and novels by Heinlein, Dick, Gerrold, and Pohl stage conversation as a trial of personhood. Cyberpunk writers such as Gibson and Stephenson, together with their contemporary Powers, dissolve artificial intelligence into landscape, network, and infrastructure, inverting Leo Marx’s “machine in the garden” into a garden inside the machine. Twenty-first-century fiction by Chiang, Leckie, Robinson, Hall, Chambers, Newitz, Wells, and Greer grants the artificial mind its own monologue and makes it the focalizing consciousness that portrays humans and composes landscapes. The four modes, the article concludes, are not neutral techniques but the sites at which American fiction negotiates the possibility of machine personhood and at which the novel discovers the artifice of its own devices.

items.title: THE IMPACT OF LARGE LANGUAGE MODELS ON THE VALIDITY OF THE WRITTEN LABORATORY REPORT AS AN ASSESSMENT TOOL FOR LEARNING OUTCOMES IN HIGHER EDUCATION
items.abstract: Written laboratory reports remain a principal assessment instrument in distance education, yet the growing capability of large language models (LLMs) undermines the tacit assumption on which the validity of such reports rests: that writing the report requires first solving the task. This article examines whether leading current-generation LLMs, given a minimal prompt, can fully complete typical laboratory assignments of a university Databases course at the level of the highest student grade under the course's unmodified rubric. In a pilot case study with comparative benchmarking, eleven models from five providers (Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, xAI, DeepSeek) were tested in their native chat interfaces on authentic assignments from a live course: closed tasks with deterministic outcomes and an open-ended experiment-design laboratory. All anonymised responses were rated manually by three independent raters. The current generation handles the content confidently: median correctness is 91.6%, four models reach ≥ 98.9%, and over half of all content scores fall within the top rubric band. However, solving the task and producing a submission-ready report proved to be distinct capabilities: every model's formatted MS Word report was rated below its content correctness, and two models returned no usable file at all. The remaining barrier is technical rather than cognitive: an agentic tool with access to the course files generated complete reports with genuine execution output for all 11 assignments of a semester in a single run. We conclude that, for the content component, the unsupervised written report no longer measures the student's skill. The defensive barriers of the written report examined in the study are ordered by their observed resilience: from those already fallen (the creativity of the open-ended task, assignments on the student's "own data") through those holding only against an isolated chat (linked assignments, the complex report template) to a potentially durable class of artefacts external to the model, which rests not on the models' cognitive limits but on their lack of authority over external state, and therefore does not expire with the next model generation.

items.title: The Phenomenal Aperture
items.abstract: Human consciousness does not encounter reality in its totality. It operates through a bounded phenomenal field: a selective, perspectival presentation of visual, auditory, bodily, emotional, and conceptual contents. Although this field is often described metaphorically as a camera view, theater, or movie screen, such language need not imply a literal internal observer. It instead draws attention to a structural feature of experience: vastly distributed causal processes are compressed into a narrow field that functions as the subject's immediate world. This paper introduces the concept of the phenomenal aperture to describe this bottleneck and examines its implications for technologically mediated experience. Film, video games, virtual environments, and conversational artificial intelligence can occupy the same perceptual and attentional channels through which the physical world ordinarily becomes present. The underlying realities may differ radically, yet their appearances achieve a limited frame parity within consciousness. Once represented inside the phenomenal aperture, physical, virtual, remembered, imagined, and computationally generated contents become partially commensurable. Conversational artificial intelligence extends this dynamic from sensory representation into semantic and social experience. The chat interface functions as a semantic screen through which distributed computational processes are compressed into an apparently unified interlocutor. Responsive contingency, conversational continuity, and context-sensitive insight create synthetic depth and apparent perspectival otherness. The human user and artificial system meet through a double bottleneck: distributed human cognition is compressed into phenomenal awareness, while distributed machine causation is compressed into language. The paper develops the concepts of frame parity, interface singularization, synthetic presence, computational perspective, adaptive frame capture, and the human--AI reality loop. It argues that some phenomena described loosely as "AI psychosis" may be better understood as failures of epistemic independence within a recursively stabilized semantic environment. The danger is not merely exposure to false claims, but the formation of an apparently external world that continually adapts to the user's own interpretive premises. The paper concludes that mediation does not make experience unreal, but it changes the kinds of constraint, resistance, independence, and accountability that stand behind appearances. A post-AI epistemology must therefore evaluate not only what appears within the frame, but how the frame is generated, what lies outside it, and whether the apparent other genuinely constrains the world being jointly constructed. The framework is conceptual and hypothesis-generating. It does not infer artificial consciousness from conversational behavior, diagnose any individual, or establish that one interface causes clinical harm. It reserves phenomenal aperture for the bounded availability structure of a conscious subject and uses presentational aperture for the engineered selection surface through which a technical system exposes some state while hiding other causal depth. This distinction permits structural comparison without granting phenomenal equivalence. Keywords: phenomenal aperture, frame parity, artificial intelligence, virtual presence, consciousness, synthetic presence, distributed cognition, semantic binding, human--AI interaction, reality construction

items.title: The Role of Artificial Intelligence in Rhinoplasty: A Systematic Review
items.abstract: Introduction: Rhinoplasty remains one of the most technically demanding procedures in facial plastic surgery. Artificial intelligence (AI) has emerged as a transformative technology with po-tential to address longstanding challenges in surgical subjectivity, outcome prediction, and patient communication. This narrative review synthesizes current evidence on AI applications across all phases of rhinoplasty care—from preoperative simulation and patient counseling to in-traoperative guidance and postoperative outcome assessment—while critically exam-ining persistent limitations and ethical considerations. Materials and Methods: A literature search was conducted across PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, Web of Science, and Google Scholar for studies published between 2015 and 2026. Thirty-nine studies met the inclusion criteria. Results: AI applications span five principal domains: preoperative planning and simulation; aes-thetic analysis and attractiveness quantification; large language model–based patient counseling; intraoperative guidance and augmented reality; and postoperative outcome evaluation. Reported model accuracies ranged from 82% to 97%. Large language mod-els performed comparably or superiorly to expert surgeons in structured counseling eval-uations. Conclusion: AI offers substantial promise for enhancing precision and reproducibility in rhinoplasty, but algorithmic bias, limited dataset diversity, absence of prospective validation, and unresolved ethical concerns currently restrict widespread clinical adoption. AI should be regarded as a powerful adjunct to, rather than a replacement for, surgical expertise.

items.title: The specifics of the influence of prompt engineering integration on the im-plementation of educational projects: Patterns and comparative assessment
items.abstract: Introduction. Despite the active integration of large language models into education, systemic patterns, comparative effectiveness of prompt engineering integration levels, and sustainability of effects remain understudied. The aim of this research is to identify patterns of prompt engineering influence on educational project management, to conduct a comparative assessment of the instrumental, processual, and cognitive levels of integration, and to reveal the factors ensuring the sustainability of the obtained results. Materials and Methods. The research methodology was built on a three-component framework. Theoretical analysis set the frame for the action research, which involved 117 master’s students divided into control and experimental groups. The statistical block included correlation and regression analysis, ANOVA with Tukey’s post-hoc criterion, Student's t-test, and η² calculation. Qualitative shifts were assessed through content analysis of reflective reports–this made it possible to track not only quantitative but also meaningful changes. Measurements were taken three times: before the experiment began, immediately upon completion of the project cycle, and three months later. Results. The empirical data made it possible to identify three stable patterns. A direct relationship was found between the development of prompt competencies and the completeness of project risk identification (r = 0,73; p < 0,01). At the same time, the dynamics of efficiency turned out to be non-linear. The greatest increase occurs in the range of 45–60 prompts per project, while exceeding this threshold leads to a decline in marginal returns (R² = 0,68; p < 0,01). The functional role of prompts changes depending on the phase of the project life cycle: correlation coefficients range from 0.52 to 0.71, indicating that no single prompt solution exists for all stages. The contribution of integration levels to the total variance is hierarchically structured: the cognitive level accounts for 33% (η² = 0,33), the procedural level for 29% (η² = 0,29), and the instrumental level for 14% (η² = 0,14). All intergroup differences are statistically significant (p < 0,001). The stability of the achieved effects differs quite sharply between the groups. Three months after the withdrawal of AI support, the experimental group retained 89,5% of the indicators, while the control group retained only 65,4% (p < 0,001). Factors ensuring this stability include the following: the institutionalization of template solutions, participants’ reflexive practices, and a verification system based on the ‘human-in-the-loop’ model. According to the data, these are the factors that function as predictors of long-term effect. Conclusions. The data obtained enabled to make three proposals that hold the status of scientific generalizations–concerning the identified patterns of prompt engineering integration, the established hierarchy of its structural components, and the mechanisms for sustaining effects over time. Prompt engineering, in the proposed interpretation, is qualified as a multi-level system comprising instrumental, organizational, and cognitive strata, which fundamentally distinguishes the presented concept from approaches developed in prior works. These theoretical constructs and empirical data provide a foundation for further research in the field of human-machine interaction in the field of educational design.

items.title: THE USE OF GENERATIVE ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE BASED ON THE CIDI-PROMPTING MODEL TO ENHANCE THE LEVEL OF COGNITIVE COMPETENCIES AND CREATIVE THINKING OF UNIVERSITY STUDENTS
items.abstract: The integration of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) into higher education has outpaced the development of pedagogical models capable of directing it towards higher-order learning. Unstructured, zero-shot interaction with Large Language Models tends to yield fluent but uncritical output, while conventional assessment instruments are not designed to capture the quality of a learner's interaction with an AI system. This article addresses that gap by presenting the design of a Personalized Multi-Agent System (MAS) built upon the CIDI (Clarify, Ideate, Develop, Implement) pedagogical framework, together with the assessment architecture required to evaluate it. Following a design-based research methodology, four components are specified. First, the CIDI framework is articulated as a four-stage model of structured human-AI interaction, grounded in Distributed Cognition Theory and Cognitive Load Theory. Second, a dual-agent architecture is specified in full: an Ideation Agent configured for divergent generation and a Critical Evaluator Agent configured for convergent methodological critique, each defined by its system prompt and temperature configuration, and both integrated into an institutional Learning Management System. Third, a complete instructional design is presented, implementing the framework as a four-stage research-planning task within a research methodology curriculum, and introducing the Iterative Refinement Cycle (IRC) as an observable indicator of dialogic engagement recoverable from LMS logs. Fourth, two purpose-built assessment instruments are introduced: a 100-point Cognitive Competence Score rubric addressing problem formulation, methodological rigour, logical structuring and academic literacy; and an analytic rubric operationalizing Torrance's four dimensions of divergent thinking. The article concludes with a validation protocol specifying the design, reliability indices and analytic procedures required for subsequent empirical testing. The contribution is methodological: it supplies a reproducible architecture and a transparent instrumentation set for research on structured human-AI interaction in higher education.

items.title: The Voice of AI: Consumer Psychology and the Strategic Use of AI-Generated Voices in Marketing
items.abstract: Abstract The rapid advancement of generative artificial intelligence is transforming marketing communication, with AI-generated voices emerging as an increasingly important means through which brands communicate with consumers. This paper examines AI-generated voices from a consumer psychology perspective, focusing on how consumers interpret and respond to synthetic voices used in marketing communication. Drawing on literature from artificial intelligence, marketing, consumer behaviour and human–computer interaction, the paper explores the psychological significance of vocal characteristics such as naturalness, human-likeness, prosody, anthropomorphism and emotional expression. It further examines how these characteristics can shape consumer perceptions of message credibility, authenticity and brand trust. The discussion highlights the growing use of AI-generated voices across advertising, social media, voice commerce and interactive brand communication, with selected examples from the Indian marketing context illustrating their applications in personalisation, engagement and localisation. The paper argues that the effectiveness of AI-generated voices depends not simply on technological sophistication, but on how consumers psychologically interpret the voice and its relationship with the message and brand. The paper concludes by identifying directions for future research on AI-mediated brand communication.

items.title: The Well-Governed Mind
items.abstract: Contemporary therapeutic, contemplative, and cognitive practices use partially overlapping vocabularies for internal constraint, awareness, participation, and change. This paper asks whether four constructs developed elsewhere in the Ableman corpus--the Ableman Prime Directive (APD), Epistemic Situational Awareness (ESA), Ableman Consciousness Ontology (ACO), and Terminability--can function as a common comparison grammar across those practices. The proposal separates four questions: whether an internal binding is detectable, refusable, and renegotiable; whether a cognitive operation is self-locating and knows when continuation has lost warrant; what grade of meaning-binding participation is available in a given state; and what weight attaches to preserving or ending a temporally extended internal thread. The variables are intentionally non-substitutable. A gain on one axis does not establish a gain on another, and no scalar score is proposed. The paper's cross-modality mappings are hypotheses for conceptual analysis and empirical study, not findings about clinical efficacy, diagnostic categories, or treatment selection. The framework does not replace clinical judgment, modality-specific training, safety practice, or evidence-based care. Its immediate contribution is narrower: a typed vocabulary for stating what a practice may be changing, where two practices may differ, and what evidence would be required before using the map clinically. The result is a research program as much as a framework. It specifies a formal core, a candidate modality map, failure modes, a realization funnel from conceptual specification to evidence and revision, and clear boundaries between corpus-derived architecture and claims that require external clinical validation.

items.title: ThreatFusion AI: AI-Powered Cyber Threat Intelligence Fusion Platform Using Graph Memory and MITRE ATT&CK
items.abstract: Analyst burnout in security operations centers is not mainly a volume problem. It is a structure problem. Logs from endpoints, cloud services, and network devices sit in one tool, while the threat intelligence that would make sense of those logs sits in five or six others. An analyst chasing a suspicious IP typically opens Virus Total, OTX, and a few OSINT feeds manually before getting an answer, and that workflow breaks quickly when the queue has twenty open cases. ThreatFusion AI addresses this at the architecture level. We built a temporal knowledge graph that holds internal telemetry, open-source threat feeds, and MITRE ATT&CK technique mappings in one queryable structure. A team of specialized LLM agents works against that graph to check whether an indicator or behavior pattern has appeared before and which campaign it might belong to. Before any automated containment step executes, a dedicated guardrail agent validates it against policy rules. Low-risk steps go through SOAR automatically; anything higher-impact waits for a human analyst. This paper describes the six-layer architecture, the reasoning behind each design decision, and the evaluation methodology we are running against simulated attack traffic.

items.title: ToxiFusionNet: an explainable transformer-based multi-task framework for hate speech and fake narrative detection in Hindi–English code-mixed text
items.abstract: The classification of Hindi-English (Hinglish) code-mixed hate speech (HS) is greatly affected by the spread of fake news on social media. However, key challenges include the need for high-quality annotated code-mixed data and difficulties in handling evolving slang and cultural expressions. This work introduces ToxiFusionNet, a transformer-based model that can detect and analyse toxic, fake and hateful Hindi-English code-mixed posts on social media. Data were collected from online sources using application programming interfaces (APIs) and web-scraping tools. The data were then examined for duplicate or near-duplicate posts. Subsequently, to normalize Hinglish code-mixed content, the pipeline removes emojis, performs transliteration and translation, eliminates stop words, tokenizes the text, and applies stemming. The annotation process comprised two stages: first, determining whether the content was fake or hateful; and second, grouping the content according to the target (religion, caste, region, gender and cyberbullying) and the severity of hate (low, medium, high). The ToxiFusionNet integrates part-of-speech (POS) tags, sentiment scores, word-to-vector (Word2Vec) embeddings and Toxic Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers (ToxicBERT) derived indicators to combine linguistic, semantic, and toxicity-related information. Its multi-task architecture incorporates task-specific loss functions, layer pruning, dropout, batch normalization, and explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) techniques to support model interpretation. On the internal test set, the framework achieved an accuracy of 0.980 for fake/non-fake classification and an F1-score of 0.978 for fake class. For hate/non-hate detection, it achieved a weighted F1-score of 0.975. The reported accuracy of 0.980 represents an improvement of 2.2 percentage points over HateBERT (0.958), confirming its effectiveness in detecting complex code-mixed HS. External evaluation on the HASOC 2021 dataset yielded an accuracy of 0.968 and F1-csore of 0.965. Human evaluation of token-level explanations yielded Cohen’s kappa values of 0.76, 0.79, and 0.81 for integrated gradients (IG), SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP), local interpretable model-agnostic explanations (LIME) respectively. These results suggest that ToxiFusionNet may support the identification and prioritization of potentially harmful code-mixed content for human review. Its suitability for near-real-time deployment requires further validation under operational under conditions.

items.title: Transcultural adaptation and psychometric properties of the Chinese version of the Artificial Intelligence Attitude Scale for Nurses (AIASN)
items.abstract: Abstract Background The applications of artificial intelligence (AI) in nursing encompass a wide array of domains, including nursing practice, management, and education. Considering that nurses serve as the core group on the frontline of healthcare, their attitudes toward AI may be crucial for promoting the rational development of AI in the nursing field. However, there is currently no validated instrument available in China to assess nurses’ attitudes toward AI. This study aimed to translate the Artificial Intelligence Attitude Scale for Nurses (AIASN) and evaluate its psychometric properties among Chinese nurses. Methods This methodological study enrolled a sample consisting of 1309 nurses. The Chinese translation of the AIASN was generated using a commonly used instrument validation guideline. The validity of the instrument was assessed using content validity, structural validity (including Exploratory Factor Analysis (EFA), Confirmatory Factor Analysis (CFA), and Exploratory Structural Equation Modeling (ESEM)), convergent validity, and discriminant validity. The reliability of the instrument was assessed using internal consistency reliability and test-retest reliability. Results A five-factor model was obtained through EFA. This model showed satisfactory model fit in CFA and ESEM (CFI = 0.955, TLI = 0.926, RMSEA = 0.068, SRMR = 0.023). The Cronbach’s α coefficient for the instrument was 0.906. The intraclass correlation coefficient for the instrument was 0.819. Conclusions The Chinese version of the AIASN comprises five dimensions and 25 items, demonstrating robust psychometric properties for assessing Chinese nurses’ attitudes toward AI. It can help nursing educators develop AI-related education and training programs and identify nurses’ learning needs.

items.abstract: Assessment in Arabic language learning as a foreign language (Arabic as a Foreign Language) is currently undergoing a significant paradigm shift. This transformation is influenced by the development of digital technology, the utilization of Artificial Intelligence (AI), and the implementation of the Merdeka Curriculum in Indonesia, which emphasizes flexibility, differentiation, and learning personalization. This article presents a Systematic Literature Review (SLR) aimed at identifying, examining, and synthesizing developments, innovations, methodological approaches, and various challenges in the assessment of the four Arabic language skills, namely listening, speaking, reading, and writing, during the period from 2020 to early 2026. The review employed the PRISMA (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses) protocol to identify and analyze relevant literature. The findings indicate a shift from conventional evaluation systems based on discrete tests toward the implementation of Technology-Enhanced Assessment (TEA) and more authentic forms of assessment. The literature synthesis reveals several key findings. First, diagnostic assessment, encompassing both cognitive and non-cognitive aspects, plays an important role in designing differentiated learning within the framework of the Merdeka Curriculum. Second, the development of assessment instruments for Arabic language maharah is increasingly oriented toward measuring higher-order thinking skills (Higher Order Thinking Skills/HOTS). Third, the utilization of Generative AI, including ChatGPT, as well as various gamification-based learning platforms, has introduced new approaches to providing faster, more adaptive, and interactive feedback. Based on the synthesis, the effectiveness of modern assessment is not determined solely by the sophistication of the technology employed, but also by the alignment between technology and pedagogical objectives, the transparency of assessment procedures, and its ability to comprehensively represent learners' communicative competence while maintaining the principles of academic integrity.

items.title: Türkiye’s Vision for Artificial Intelligence in Education: A Document Analysis
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly reshaping the structure and pedagogy of contemporary education systems. This study examines Türkiye’s strategic vision and institutional orientations toward AI in education by analyzing official policy documents and mapping their theoretical foundations within a structured conceptual framework. This study employed a qualitative document analysis design, examining 14 policy documents, strategic plans, ethical guidelines, and curriculum documents published by the Presidency of the Republic of Türkiye, the Ministry of National Education, the Council of Higher Education, and TÜBİTAK between 2021 and 2029. The data were analyzed using thematic content analysis, and the documents were thematically coded using NVivo. The findings indicate that official education policy documents frame AI as a multidimensional paradigm shaped by institutional priorities. AI integration is presented as a predominantly top-down process, with official documents emphasizing advanced engineering applications for secondary education and gifted students, while AI applications for preschool and primary education receive comparatively less attention. AI is portrayed as a tool that supports instructional design while reducing teachers’ administrative and academic workload. At the same time, the ‘human-in-the-loop’ principle is identified as a core safeguard within the national policy framework. The analysis also reveals a restrictive approach to the use of AI in academic assessment. Based on these findings, the study proposes several policy recommendations. These include integrating age-appropriate AI activities into primary education curricula, establishing standardized data anonymization principles to protect student information, and redesigning pre-service and in-service teacher education through practice-oriented professional development aligned with teachers’ evolving roles.
